lede: A 2014 method turns a protein into counts of residue pairs at each distance and hands them to an SVM. Its software is gone. We ported the SVM from its C source and ran it again on the same benchmark. SVM-DR came back: its Table 1 ROC, nine of ten points of Fig. 3, and its discriminant weights in Figs 4B, 5C and 5D. SVM-DT needs profiles from a database that no longer exists. Rebuilt the way the lab's 2008 paper made them, they bring back its family-level results, while its average ROC lands about 0.01 above the paper's.
matched_intro: The figures were drawn with tools we do not have, so we keep the published frame, ticks, labels and legends and draw only the data, at sizes measured from the figure. Fig. 3 points sit on an axis map fitted to the tick marks. Fig. 4 cells take the grey of the published colour bar. Fig. 5 bars sit at x = d + 1, where the published bars are.
matched: The 54 SCOP 1.53 families of Liao and Noble, the feature vectors of the paper's Eq. 1 and 2, and Gist 2.3 ported from its C source with its default settings.
Identical sequences can give a normalized kernel value one rounding step above 1, which Gist sets to 0. That breaks training. We set it to 1, and the published weights come back.

Built as in the lab's 2008 Top-n-gram paper, which the paper cites: PSI-BLAST 2.17 with default settings and 10 iterations against the lab's 2016 nrdb90, then BLOSUM62 pseudocounts. The paper's own database is not known.
Overlay: ink is the paper only, light green is the reproduction only, dark green is both. Difference: darker means a larger grey difference.
claims_line: The main claim holds: pair distances add to a position-independent baseline, and SVM-DR comes back as published. The claims that do not match trace to the ROC50 definition and to the regenerated profiles.
closing: SVM-DR came back from the paper alone, all but its ROC50. SVM-DT came back at the family level; its averages sit a little above the paper's, and its profile database is gone.
roc50_note: Our ROC matches the paper's at every dMAX, so our rankings of the test proteins agree with the authors'. ROC50 is computed from those same rankings, so the gap comes from how the paper computed ROC50, not from the method. With the standard definition (Gribskov and Robinson's area up to the first 50 false positives) we get {dr50} for SVM-DR and {dt50} for SVM-DT. The paper's values match a non-standard reading: an ordinary ROC computed on the ranking cut at the 50th false positive, which divides by the positives found there instead of by all positives (0.712 against 0.715 for SVM-DR; for SVM-DT 0.838 against 0.800, above as its ROC is). The paper gives no ROC50 code to confirm it. Other readings tested do not fit (see the README's ROC50 section).
dt_note: SVM-DT is rerun on regenerated profiles. The paper's 2014 profile database no longer exists, so we built the profiles the way the paper's reference [28] describes (10 PSI-BLAST iterations, BLOSUM62 pseudocounts) against the lab's 2016 nrdb90. Everything after the profiles is the code that reproduces SVM-DR's panels almost exactly. These profiles bring back family 2.5.1.3 (ROC 0.993, as published) and the order of its top pairs, and move Figs 4A and 5A-B closer than the lab's later 3-iteration settings did. The 54-family average lands about 0.01 above the paper at every dMAX ({dt_roc} against {dt_paper}), which we put down to the database, untested. These items are marked Re-measured.
